newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka tightens security as violence mars polls.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka tightens security as violence mars polls.

text.p: A bomb rocked a village and fighting was reported in many parts of Sri Lanka on Friday as islanders voted in council elections seen as the first political test for the government of President Chandrika Kumaratunga.

Sri Lankan authorities, acting to prevent post-election violence, tightened security soon after polling closed at 4:00 p.m. (1000 GMT), officials said. First results were likely to be announced around 10:00 p.m. (1600 GMT), but a clear picture would emerge only on Saturday morning.
A military official said the army had begun patrolling the streets in Colombo and in some troubled towns in the island to prevent mobs going on the rampage.
"The situation in Colombo has been calm so far. We don't expect any outbreaks of violence," Colombo's police chief D.M. Dissanayake told Reuters.
Colombo streets were near deserted on Friday afternoon with shops and offices putting up shutters long before polling closed.
The defence ministry said a precautionary night curfew was being imposed in Colombo and southern Kalutara and Gampaha districts from 10 p.m. (1600 GMT).
About 70 violent incidents were reported overnight before polling began at 8,246 stations, the police elections secretariat said.
The Centre for Monitoring Election Violence, an independent group, said it had recorded about 200 incidents of poll-related violence between Thursday night and Friday.
Most of them were clashes between supporters of the ruling People's Alliance (PA) and the opposition United National Party (UNP), the main contenders in the election.

Police said 10 people were injured, four seriously, when a bomb exploded early on Friday morning near a polling station in Koswatte village in the northcentral Puttalam district, 50 km (30 miles) from Colombo.
"A People's Alliance candidate has complained, accusing United National Party supporters of having thrown the bomb," an official at the elections secretariat told Reuters.
An Elections Department official said initial reports from polling stations indicated voter turnout of about 60 to 65 percent.
"But this figure can change as we go on. Voter turnout in Colombo was fairly high, but fairly low in some outstation centres," the official said.
UNP spokesman Irvin Weerackody said the party's polling agents had been driven from election centres by PA activists in several areas, including in the capital Colombo.
But Colombo and its suburbs, which have been centres of violence during previous elections, were largely peaceful and saw brisk voting, election workers said.

"We are counting on a high voter turnout," said opposition leader and former prime minister Ranil Wickremesinghe after casting his vote in Colombo. "If it is a free and fair election, the UNP will win."
Some 10 million Sri Lankans were eligible to vote to elect 3,567 representatives to 238 local bodies.
Voter turnout in Sri Lanka's last general election in 1994 was 76 percent.

The Election Office says more than 100,000 public servants manned 8,246 polling stations across the island except in the northern and eastern provinces where government troops are fighting Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam Tamil (LTTE) rebels.
